title: Analytics, Data & Attribution
excerpt: Tracking, dashboards and attribution that connect ad spend to revenue, decisions from data, not gut feel. See how it works.
rm_desc: Marketing analytics, dashboards and attribution that connect ad spend to revenue. See how it works.
content: Marketing analytics exists to answer one question: which channels actually drive revenue? Without it, every budget decision is a guess. We build the measurement layer first: tracking, unified reporting and attribution that connect marketing activity to funded outcomes.
• Conversion tracking, tag management and analytics integration (GA4, Looker)
• CRM data connectivity: marketing joined to sales outcomes
• Unified dashboards across paid platforms, analytics and CRM
• Attribution and funnel analysis across the full customer journey, held honestly: every attribution model is an estimate, so we triangulate models rather than worship one
• Continuous optimisation cycles driven by the data

For a national sports and entertainment precinct we grew the addressable audience from 53k to 745k defined individuals using cookieless personas, and ongoing campaigns against those segments run 20–30% better on CPA with platform-reported ROAS above 400%, platform-reported deliberately said aloud, since ROAS a platform grades for itself flatters; incrementality is the harder, better question, and we will tell you when a number is which. The audience work made the media work.
Analytics underpins our paid media and SEO & GEO / AIO / AEO engagements; it can also stand alone when the tracking is the problem.

Almost every account we open has the same fault somewhere: a conversion event firing twice, a UTM convention nobody’s followed since the person who set it up left, or a CRM field that marketing and sales define differently. Small individually, compounding badly, since every downstream report inherits the error. Google’s own GA4 setup documentation is a reasonable first check before trusting any dashboard built on top of it.

No attribution model is the truth, each one is a lens with a bias built in: last-click favours bottom-funnel channels, first-click favours awareness, and models built on account data inherit whatever pattern the platform’s black box decided to weight. Our marketing analytics work reports more than one model side by side rather than picking a favourite and presenting it as fact, and labels platform-reported numbers as platform-reported, since a platform grading its own performance has an obvious incentive to grade generously.
What marketing analytics costs to set up properly

The honest range is wide because the starting point varies so much. A business with clean GA4 tracking and a modern CRM needs weeks of integration work. A business running on spreadsheets and an untagged website needs a foundation rebuild before any dashboard is trustworthy, and that foundation work is where most of the budget goes, not the dashboard itself, which is comparatively quick to build once the data underneath it is sound. Anyone quoting a flat price without first auditing your current stack is guessing at the harder half of the job.
Signs your marketing analytics needs a rebuild

A few reliable tells: two reports in the building disagree on the same number and nobody can explain why; a channel gets credited with conversions that other data suggests it did not drive; or decisions get made from gut feel because nobody trusts the dashboard enough to act on it. Any one of those is worth a proper audit before the next quarter's budget gets set on assumptions rather than evidence.
Who owns marketing analytics once it is built

Dashboards decay without an owner. Tracking breaks silently when a site update ships, a new campaign type launches without a UTM convention, or a CRM field gets renamed. We hand over documentation and a maintenance checklist at the end of setup, but the accounts that stay clean longest are the ones where someone internally is named as the owner, not left as everyone's shared responsibility, which in practice means nobody's.
